descricao: Family vocabulary organized by generation and relationship — nuclear family, extended family, the four prefixes that build complex relationships, and the words that trap Portuguese speakers.

secoes.conteudo:
Family vocabulary is often some of the first English anyone learns. Mother. Father. Brother. Sister. These are A1 words. But real conversations go much further. How do you say 'sobrinha'? What about 'cunhado'? Or 'padrasto'? English has all of these — and they follow patterns that make them easy to learn once you see the logic.

In this material, you will learn family vocabulary in two ways. First, by generation: the people at each level of a family tree, always in pairs — parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren. Then, by prefix: four short additions to existing words that create dozens of new relationships without requiring dozens of new words. By the end, you will be able to describe any family structure — traditional, modern, or complex — in natural English.

secoes.titulo: The Nuclear Family: Parents / Children, Husband / Wife
secoes.conteudo:
At the center of most family trees: the **nuclear family** — the small, immediate unit of parents and children living together.

Your **parents** are your mother and father — specifically and only them. This matters enormously, as we will see in the trap words section. A **mother** and a **father** — often shortened in everyday speech to **mum** (British English) or **mom** (American English), and **dad** in both. These informal words are far more common in real conversation than 'mother' and 'father,' which sound more formal or emotional.

Your **son** is your male child; your **daughter** is your female child. Together, they are your **children** — one **child**, many **children**, an essential irregular plural. And between children: **brothers** and **sisters**. English has one more word that covers both without specifying gender: **sibling**. 'Do you have any siblings?' is one of the most common early conversation questions in English. 'I have three siblings' tells you how many, without saying how many of each. A genuinely useful word.

For the married pair: **husband** and **wife**. The formal, gender-neutral word for either one is **spouse** — used on official forms and in writing when gender is not specified. In everyday conversation, people use **husband** or **wife**, or increasingly, **partner** — a flexible word that works for any committed relationship, married or not.

secoes.titulo: The Extended Family: Grandparents / Grandchildren, Uncle / Nephew, Aunt / Niece
secoes.conteudo:
Moving outward from the nuclear family, the next layer follows a pattern of doubled and mirrored titles.

Your parents' parents are your **grandparents** — your **grandfather** and **grandmother**. In informal, everyday speech, these become **grandpa** and **grandma**, or **grandad** and **nan** in some British families. Your own children's children, one day, will be your **grandchildren** — your **grandson** and **granddaughter**. **Grandparents** and **grandchildren** are the natural pair: one generation up, one generation down, each with the same prefix and structure.

Your parents' siblings form the next pair. Your parent's brother is your **uncle**. Your parent's sister is your **aunt**. Their children are your **cousins** — and here English is simpler than Portuguese: there is no different word for male or female cousins. Everyone is simply a **cousin**. If you need to specify gender, you say 'my male cousin' or 'my female cousin,' but in practice this is rare.

And then the mirror image: your own siblings' children. Your sibling's son is your **nephew**. Your sibling's daughter is your **niece**. **Nephew** and **niece** are always learned as a pair — if you know one, you immediately understand why the other exists. Say them together a few times: nephew and niece. They go together always.

secoes.titulo: Prefixes That Build New Relationships: Step- / Half-, Great- / In-Law
secoes.conteudo:
Here is where English family vocabulary becomes genuinely elegant. Instead of inventing new words for every complex relationship, English uses four simple prefixes. Once you know them, dozens of new words become immediately readable.

**Great-** means one generation further back than expected. Your grandparents are one generation above your parents. Add **great-** and you go back one more: your **great-grandparents** are your grandparents' parents. Their siblings are your **great-uncles** and **great-aunts**. Each additional **great-** takes you back one more generation: **great-great-grandparents**, and so on, as far back as anyone needs to go.

**In-law** signals family through marriage — not through blood, but through your husband or wife. Your partner's parents become your **in-laws** — specifically your **father-in-law** and **mother-in-law**. Their siblings are your **brother-in-law** and **sister-in-law**. The order is fixed: the family title always comes first, **-in-law** always at the end. The plural works on the person, not the suffix: **mothers-in-law**, not 'mother-in-laws' — though in informal speech, you will hear both.

**Step-** describes family through a parent's new marriage — a relationship that is legal and social, but not biological. If your mother marries a new man, he becomes your **stepfather**. His children from a previous relationship become your **stepbrothers** and **stepsisters**.

**Half-** means sharing only one birth parent. A **half-sister** shares your father but has a different mother, or shares your mother but has a different father. The connection is biological — but through only one parent. The distinction between **step-** and **half-** is important: **step-** is through marriage; **half-** is through shared blood from one parent.

secoes.titulo: Types of Family and Key Life Events
secoes.conteudo:
English has specific words for different family structures, and for the moments that build and change them.

An **immediate family** is the small, close circle — usually just parents and children. An **extended family** is the full picture: grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins, everyone connected by blood or marriage. A **nuclear family** is the traditional structure: two parents and their children under one roof. A **blended family** forms when two people come together and bring children from previous relationships — a mix of **stepsiblings**, possibly new children together, all living as one household. A **single parent** raises children without a live-in partner.

For the events that build and change families: two people may **get engaged** — they formally agree to marry. The **engagement** is the period between that promise and the wedding. When they **get married**, they become a **married couple**. If the marriage ends legally, they **get divorced**. You say 'they got divorced' for the event, and 'they are divorced' for the current state.

One more word that comes up often in personal stories: **raised**. To **raise** a child means to care for them as they grow up. 'She was raised by her grandparents' means her grandparents were the ones who took care of her throughout her childhood — they were her primary family, regardless of who her birth parents were. **Raised** is the word that captures this most naturally in English.

Here is a grammar point that is simple but genuinely useful: how to describe a family relationship when you do not know or cannot remember the specific word.

English uses possessive -'s chains to explain any relationship. 'My father's sister' = my aunt. 'My mother's brother' = my uncle. 'My brother's daughter' = my niece. 'My sister's son' = my nephew. 'My father's father' = my grandfather.

This matters for two reasons. First, if you forget a specific word — say, 'niece' — you can describe your way around it and still be perfectly understood: 'my sister's daughter.' Second, thinking this way trains you to understand relationships structurally, which makes the specific vocabulary easier to remember.

The apostrophe-s in English signals possession: 'my father's sister' means 'the sister who belongs to my father's side.' This structure is very flexible — you can chain as many steps as needed. 'My mother's brother's son' = my cousin. Long chains are unusual in conversation, but for explaining a complex relationship in the moment, they always work.

One more note: in English, you can also explain relationships using 'on my mother's side' or 'on my father's side.' 'My uncle on my mother's side' means your mother's brother. This phrase appears often when you want to clarify which branch of the family someone comes from.

Two traps in family vocabulary cause consistent misunderstanding, and they are both about the same fundamental confusion.

**Parents** and **parentes**. This is one of the most important false friends in English for Portuguese speakers. **Parents** in English means exclusively your mother and father — those two people, nobody else. It does not mean relatives or family members in general. For that, English uses **relatives** or **family**. 'My parents are coming to visit' = meus pais vêm visitar. 'My relatives are coming to visit' = minha família / meus parentes virão visitar. Confusing these two produces a very specific misunderstanding: the listener will picture your mother and father, when you may be referring to your cousins, your aunt, your entire extended family.

**Sibling**. In Portuguese, there is no single gender-neutral word for irmão or irmã — you always specify. English has **sibling**, which covers both without indicating gender. 'Do you have any siblings?' is asking whether you have brothers, sisters, or both. 'I have two siblings' tells you the number without the gender. This word feels strange to Portuguese speakers at first, because the concept of a gender-neutral word for brothers and sisters simply does not exist in their language. But it is widely used in English and will make you sound natural.

**Cousin**. In Portuguese, 'primo' and 'prima' are different words. In English, a cousin is always a **cousin** — no distinction. When speakers need to specify gender, they say 'my male cousin' or 'my female cousin,' but this is rare. In everyday conversation, 'my cousin' is always enough.
